rows.question: Your bounds separated observations from assumptions. Switch to cooling: two kilograms of well-mixed water starts at sixty degrees Celsius in a room held at twenty degrees. It reaches forty degrees after ten minutes and thirty after twenty. Specific heat is four thousand two hundred joules per kilogram per kelvin. Vessel heat capacity is negligible; no evaporation or internal heating occurs. Heat-loss power equals constant conductance times water temperature minus room temperature. Derive conductance with units. [Interviewer pause: one point five seconds.] A later run starts at sixty and reaches twenty-seven after twenty minutes; its constant ambient temperature was not logged. Construct two exact explanations, one retaining conductance and one retaining twenty-degree ambient. What experiment distinguishes them?
rows.recognizedQuestion: Switch to cooling two kilograms of well mixed water starts at sixty degrees Celsius in a room held at twenty degrees It reaches forty degrees after ten minutes and thirty after twenty specific heat is four thousand two hundred joules per kilogram per kelvin. Vessel heat capacity is negligible no evaporation or internal heating occurs Heat loss power equals constant conductance times water temperature minus room temperature derive conductance with units interviewer pause one point five seconds A later run starts at sixty and reaches twenty seven after twenty minutes its constant ambient temperature was not logged Construct two exact explanations one retaining conductance and one retaining twenty degree ambient What experiment distinguishes them
rows.answer:
The original conductance is 14 ln(2) watts per kelvin, approximately 9.70 W/K. The later result can be explained exactly either by a colder room at 16°C with that same conductance, or by increased conductance at a room temperature of 20°C.

The water’s heat capacity is C = mc = 2 × 4,200 = 8,400 J/K. Conservation of energy gives
C dT/dt = −G(T − A),
where G is conductance and A is constant ambient temperature. Integrating gives
T(t) = A + (T(0) − A) exp(−Gt/C),
with time in seconds.

In the original run, the temperature excess above 20°C falls from 40 K to 20 K in 600 seconds, so
exp(−600G/8,400) = 1/2,
G = (8,400/600) ln(2) = 14 ln(2) W/K.
At twenty minutes the excess is one quarter of its initial value, predicting 20 + 40/4 = 30°C, consistent with the second observation.

For the later run, here are two exact explanations:

1. Retain the original conductance. Its twenty-minute decay factor remains 1/4. Therefore
27 = A + (60 − A)/4,
which gives A = 16°C.

2. Retain the 20°C ambient temperature. Then
27 − 20 = (60 − 20) exp(−1,200G/8,400),
so
G = 7 ln(40/7) W/K ≈ 12.20 W/K.
This is about 26% greater than the original conductance.

To distinguish them, repeat the later setup while continuously measuring both ambient and water temperatures, preferably holding the ambient at a verified 20°C. Under the unchanged-conductance explanation, the water reaches 30°C after twenty minutes; under the increased-conductance explanation, it reaches 27°C. Fit the logged cooling curve to check conductance and whether the constant-ambient model actually holds. The single later endpoint alone cannot identify both ambient temperature and conductance, and a repeat only diagnoses the earlier run if its heat-transfer conditions are reproduced.

rows.name: original-candidate-context-why
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer:
Because cooling depends on both conductance and ambient temperature, the later endpoint alone cannot tell us which changed.

The water’s heat capacity is C = mc = 2 × 4,200 = 8,400 J/K. Energy conservation gives C dT/dt = −G(T − A), so T(t) = A + (60 − A)e^(−Gt/C), with time in seconds. In the original run, the temperature excess above 20°C halves in 600 seconds, giving G = (8,400/600) ln 2 = 14 ln 2 ≈ 9.70 W/K. That also predicts 30°C at twenty minutes, matching the second observation.

For the later run, retaining that conductance makes the twenty-minute decay factor exactly 1/4. Thus 27 = A + (60 − A)/4, which gives A = 16°C. Alternatively, retaining A = 20°C gives 7 = 40e^(−1,200G/8,400), so G = 7 ln(40/7) ≈ 12.20 W/K. Both explanations reproduce 27°C exactly.

To distinguish them, measure the ambient temperature during a repeat under the later run’s conditions: the explanations predict 16°C versus 20°C. An additional water-temperature measurement at ten minutes also distinguishes these two models: they predict 38°C versus 20 + √280 ≈ 36.73°C, provided the conditions remain unchanged.
